input: It is worth noting that the contract packaging firm, which operates 2 plants and generates revenue of $80 million per year, is currently facing a number of significant operational challenges that warrant careful consideration. Drawing on a comprehensive evidence base comprising order records for 12 months and encompassing some 13,579 orders in total, on-time delivery performance over the last two quarters stood at 88%, which falls notably short of the target of 95% that the business has set for itself. In addition, overtime cost reached $1.6 million last year, representing an increase of 24% on the year before, while the order backlog currently stands at 3.3 weeks, compared with 1.8 weeks a year ago, highlighting a deteriorating position across several measures at once. A closer look at the data reveals that Plant 2 accounts for 57% of late orders, which suggests that the difficulties are concentrated rather than evenly spread across the estate. Against this backdrop, a scheduling system for all plants has been quoted at $275k, whereas Plant 2 alone would cost $120k. An internal estimate — it should be emphasized that this is not a vendor figure — suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15–20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported, with the operations director owning the scheduling programme. Overall, this phased approach would allow the firm to test the system where the need appears greatest before committing to the full $275k rollout, although it remains to be seen whether the anticipated benefits will fully materialize in practice.

The order backlog stands at 3.3 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 57% of late orders. The firm runs 2 plants with revenue of $80 million per year, and the late orders are concentrated in one plant. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $275k. Plant 2 alone costs $120k against $275k for all plants, and the narrower installation is the one the delivery record supports first. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. The estimate is untested, and no measured reduction stands behind the range. Overtime is the cost of holding delivery performance with the present schedule: crews work beyond the planned day to clear orders that the schedule did not place in time. The backlog carries the same message as the delivery figure. Work arrives faster than the schedule clears it, and the excess is absorbed by overtime and by waiting orders. None of the figures in the order records measures the scheduling system itself. The system is untested in either plant, and the first installation is also the first measurement of the reduction. Holding the remaining plants until the results are reported keeps the commitment at the single-plant cost while the estimate is unproven, and a reported result then decides the wider rollout on measured figures rather than on the estimate. Delivery performance at Plant 2 is the measured problem, the programme has a named owner, and the first installation tests the estimate.
